344.title: Lamp of beauty
344.hook: the Jaap moves into Persian: He is the glorious one, the lamp of beauty (Jaap)
344.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Jaap Sahib move through its Persian and Arabic passages each morning in the same rhythm as the rest, and the words husn (beauty) and charaag (lamp) are still familiar in Punjabi.

segments.voice: Yesterday, song of songs, and your line, the dance of dances. Did music move you a little? Today, Jaap changes language in the middle of the hymn. Day three hundred forty-four.
screen: `SONG OF SONGS — THE DANCE OF DANCES.`

segments.voice: A friend who speaks three languages is telling you a story in English. Then they reach the part they really care about, and suddenly it's Spanish, or Punjabi, or Tagalog. Some things only sound right in one language. Grandma's words. The word for that kind of evening. Partway through Jaap Sahib, the Tenth Guru does something like that. He moves into Persian, the language of poets and courts, and starts talking about beauty. Today: lamp of beauty.
screen: `A FRIEND SWITCHES LANGUAGES.` → `SOME THINGS SOUND RIGHT IN ONE.` → `JAAP SWITCHES INTO PERSIAN.`

segments.voice: In the Tenth Guru's world, Persian was the language of the Mughal court, of government papers, and of a great tradition of love poetry. The Guru knew it well; his letter to the emperor, the Zafarnama, is written in it. So when Jaap moves into Persian and Arabic words, it isn't showing off. It reaches for a language with a long habit of praising beauty. The lines here begin with a little word, ki, meaning something like: for You are. And one of them says the One is husnal charaag. Husn is beauty, the same word Punjabi still uses for a lovely face or a lovely view. Charaag, or chiragh, is a lamp, a small oil lamp of the kind that lit houses and shrines. The lamp of beauty. Think about what that picture does. A lamp isn't beautiful because of its own shape. It's beautiful because it lets you see everything else. Lamplight makes a room golden. So the line suggests that beauty itself has a source, and that every lovely thing is lit by it. In the same Persian stretch, Jaap uses names like kareem, generous, and raheem, merciful, names Muslims also use for God. The Tenth Guru brings them into Sikh morning prayer without hesitating. Jaap reaches for every language the Guru had, Braj, Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic, as if to say: no single tongue holds the One, and every tongue can praise.
screen: `PERSIAN: THE LANGUAGE OF COURTS AND POETS.` · `HUSN: BEAUTY. CHARAAG: A LAMP.` · `A LAMP LETS YOU SEE EVERYTHING ELSE.` · `KAREEM AND RAHEEM: SHARED NAMES.` · then, large: `LAMP OF BEAUTY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one beautiful thing. Look around you right now and find it. It doesn't have to be grand. The grain in a wooden table. Light on a wall. The curve of a mug handle. Someone's handwriting. Rest your eyes on it. Then notice the light that's letting you see it, a window, a lamp, a screen's glow. The beauty and the light, together. Breathe slowly, and just enjoy it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, the word of wonder. The bell holds the time.
Lamp of beauty. Husnal charaag, in Jaap's Persian lines: the One as the lamp that lets every lovely thing be seen.
Your line: lamp of beauty. Today, point out one beautiful thing to someone else, out loud, and be the lamp for a second. Day three hundred forty-four.

only Sanskrit.

345.title: The provider
345.hook: in Persian again: He is the one who gives daily bread (Jaap)
345.howItsDone: Sikhs are taught to earn honestly (kirat karni), remember the Name (naam japna) and share (vand chhakna), and every gurdwara runs a langar, a free kitchen open to everyone.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lamp of beauty, husnal charaag, and your line, lamp of beauty. Did you point out something lovely to someone? Today, the Persian lines keep going, and they come down to the kitchen table. Day three hundred forty-five.

Pick up a slice of bread and count the hands. Someone plowed a field. Someone planted the wheat, and someone else watched the sky all summer hoping it would rain. A harvester driver, a miller, a trucker on a night highway, a baker up at four, a cashier, whoever carried the bag home. One slice, and dozens of people you'll never meet. And behind them, the rain and the sun and the soil, which nobody made. Every meal is a long chain of giving. Jaap Sahib names the start of the chain. Today: the provider.
screen: `ONE SLICE OF BREAD.` → `DOZENS OF HANDS.` → `A LONG CHAIN OF GIVING.`

segments.voice: In its Persian lines, Jaap says the One is rozi dihind, the giver of daily bread, and raazak, the provider. Rozi comes from roz, a day. It means the day's portion: the food, the wages, the livelihood that keeps a household going until tomorrow. Punjabi still uses it. When people talk about earning a living, they often say rozi roti, the daily bread and the daily flatbread. Raazak is an Arabic word for the One who provides for every creature. So in the middle of all the cosmic praise, timeless, formless, sun of suns, Jaap stops at something as plain as lunch. That's very Sikh. Guru Nanak, in Japji, says there is one Giver for all living beings, and asks never to forget that One. But notice the Sikh balance. Trusting the Provider has never meant sitting and waiting. The three pillars Sikhs are taught are naam japna, remembering the Name; kirat karni, honest work; and vand chhakna, sharing what you have. You earn your bread honestly, you thank the Giver for it, and you share it. That's why every gurdwara has a langar, a free kitchen, where anyone can eat. The bread the Provider gives passes through Sikh hands and goes straight back out again, to whoever walks in the door. The chain of giving doesn't end at your plate. In Sikh practice, it runs through it. Rozi, the daily portion, comes in, and some of it goes on to someone else.
screen: `ROZI: THE DAY'S PORTION.` · `RAAZAK: THE ONE WHO PROVIDES.` · `ONE GIVER FOR ALL BEINGS.` · `EARN, THANK, SHARE: THE LANGAR.` · then, large: `DAILY BREAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank the hands behind your food. Think of the last thing you ate, or hold something you're about to eat. Trace it back, one pair of hands at a time: who sold it, who carried it, who made it, who grew it. Thank each of them silently as you go. Then go one step further back, to the rain and the sun and the soil, and rest there with your breath. If you pray, you can thank the Giver of daily bread. The bell holds the time.
The provider. Rozi dihind, raazak: in Jaap's Persian lines, the One who gives every creature its daily bread.
Your line: daily bread. Today, before one meal, pause long enough to thank one person in the chain, and if you can, pass a little of it on. Day three hundred forty-five.

346.title: Gobind, Mukand
346.hook: gobinde mukande udaare apaare: the Sustainer, the Liberator, generous, infinite (Jaap)
346.howItsDone: In gurdwaras and homes, the line gobinde mukande udaare apaare is often recited or sung together, and Gobind is one of many names for the Divine Sikhs use in prayer and kirtan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the provider, the giver of rozi, and your line, daily bread. Did you thank one pair of hands behind a meal? Today, a line with a familiar name in it. Day three hundred forty-six.

Gobinde. Mukande. Udaare. Apaare. Four words, each ending in the same open sound, like four drumbeats. Said fast, in a room reciting Jaap, the line is easy to catch even without knowing the language. And one of those four words is a name you've heard many times this year, the name of a man. It's a little like finding your teacher's name written into the song he taught you. Today: Gobind, Mukand.
screen: `GOBINDE, MUKANDE, UDAARE, APAARE.` → `FOUR WORDS LIKE FOUR DRUMBEATS.` → `A NAME YOU ALREADY KNOW.`

segments.voice: Take the four words one at a time. Gobind is a very old Indian name for the Divine, often explained as the sustainer, the one who cares for the earth and all that lives on it. It appears again and again in the Guru Granth Sahib, long before the Tenth Guru was born. Then mukand: the liberator, the one who gives mukti, freedom from everything that binds. Then udaar: generous, open-handed. Punjabi still uses it for a big-hearted person. And apaar: paar is the far shore of a river; apaar has no far shore. Infinite. So the line says: Sustainer, Liberator, Generous, Without end. Now the name. The tenth Guru was born Gobind Rai, and tradition says that at the founding of the Khalsa he became Gobind Singh. So when he writes gobinde in his own hymn, his name is right there in the praise. Sikhs don't hear that as the Guru praising himself. The Guru was clear that he was a servant of the One, and his name, like so many Indian names, was taken from a name of God. A child named for the Sustainer grows up to sing the Sustainer's praise. Then look at the pairing in the line: udaar and apaar, generous and infinite, side by side. That's the whole hope of it. Something infinite that kept to itself would be grand and far away. Something generous with limits would run out. Jaap praises the One who is both: giving, and never running out.
screen: `GOBIND: THE SUSTAINER.` · `MUKAND: THE LIBERATOR.` · `UDAAR: GENEROUS. APAAR: NO FAR SHORE.` · `GOBIND RAI, GOBIND SINGH.` · then, large: `GENEROUS AND INFINITE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one generous act. Think of someone who could use something you have: time, a compliment, a lift, a meal, a little money, your full attention. Choose one. Picture giving it, freely, without needing thanks. Breathe in, and notice how much you have. Breathe out, and let a little of it go. If you like, say the line in rhythm: gobinde, mukande, udaare, apaare. The bell holds the time.
Gobind. The Sustainer, an ancient name for the Divine, found throughout the Guru Granth Sahib, and the name the Tenth Guru was given.
Your line: generous and infinite. Today, be generous once, and give a little more than feels necessary. Day three hundred forty-six.

347.title: One form, many sights
347.hook: ek moorat anek darsan: one form seen in countless ways (Jaap, roaaval)
347.howItsDone: Sikhs recite this roaal stanza of Jaap Sahib each morning, and the idea of the world as the One's khel, play, runs through Sikh scripture and kirtan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gobind, the Sustainer, and your line, generous and infinite. Did you give a little more than felt necessary? Today, Jaap slows into longer lines, and plays with one and many. Day three hundred forty-seven.

Bedtime, and a parent is reading a story out loud. The dragon gets a deep growl. The princess gets a bright, quick voice. The old king, the narrator, the talking cat: each one sounds different, and the child in bed believes every one of them. Nothing came from outside. All those voices were in one person the whole time. Then the book closes, the light goes off, and there's just one voice again, saying goodnight. Many from one, and back to one. Jaap Sahib has a stanza that works like that. Today: one form, many sights.
screen: `ONE READER, MANY VOICES.` → `A DRAGON, A PRINCESS, A TALKING CAT.` → `THE BOOK CLOSES: ONE VOICE AGAIN.`

segments.voice: In another stretch of Jaap, in a meter called roaal, with longer, rolling lines, one stanza opens like this: ek moorat anek darsan, keen roop anek. Ek is one. Moorat is form or likeness. Anek is many, countless. Darsan is a sight, a glimpse, the word Sikhs use for seeing something holy, as when people go for darshan at the Golden Temple. So: one form, countless sights; You made forms beyond number. Then the next line: khel khel akhel khelan, ant ko phir ek. Khel is play, a game. Having played the play, beyond all play, at the end, again One. Earlier, Jaap called the One aroop, formless. Now it says the One shows itself in countless forms. Sikh readers don't hear a contradiction there. Think of the reader at bedtime: no dragon's growl of their own, and yet every voice in the story is theirs. Sikh scripture often calls the world the One's khel, the play, the great unfolding game: in that reading, every person, every animal, every grain of sand is one more voice in the same story. And then the book closes. At the end, it all folds back. Again, One. On an ordinary day, that reading can change how people look at each other. The rude driver, your sister, the stranger on the bus, the friend you think you know completely: each one, in this reading, a different voice from the same source. Same source, countless sights. And none of them is the whole picture of anyone.
screen: `EK MOORAT: ONE FORM.` · `ANEK DARSAN: COUNTLESS SIGHTS.` · `KHEL: THE WORLD AS THE ONE'S PLAY.` · `ANT KO PHIR EK: AT THE END, ONE.` · then, large: `ONE, SEEN MANY WAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a friend with fresh eyes. Picture someone you know well. Now see them from angles you usually don't: as a small child, as their parents see them, as their coworkers do, at three in the morning, on their best day. Let each picture be one more voice in their story. Then let them fold back into the one person. Same friend, many sights. Breathe with that. If you pray, you can say ek moorat anek darsan softly. The bell holds the time.
One form. Ek moorat anek darsan: one form, seen in countless ways, playing the great play and at the end, again One.
Your line: one, seen many ways. Today, with one person who annoys you, try to see one more side of them than you usually do. Day three hundred forty-seven.

348.title: Ender and sustainer of all
348.hook: sarab kaal hain, sarab paal hain: He ends all and He sustains all (Jaap)
348.howItsDone: Sikhs understand births, deaths and every change as happening within hukam, the One's order, and recite Jaap's pairing of the One who ends and keeps all things each morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, one form, many sights, and your line, one, seen many ways. Did you see one more side of someone? Today, two words that sound like opposites, held by one hand. Day three hundred forty-eight.

Walk through a forest in late autumn. The leaves are coming down, thousands of them, every one a small ending. Kick through them, and underneath you'll find dark, crumbly soil, last year's leaves, already turning into food for the tree that dropped them. The same tree is letting go and being fed, at once, by the same falling. A gardener knows this. So does anyone who has sat in a hospital where one family grieves down the hall from another holding a newborn. Endings and keepings sit close together. Jaap Sahib puts them in one breath. Today: ender and sustainer of all.
screen: `AUTUMN LEAVES COMING DOWN.` → `LAST YEAR'S LEAVES FEED THE TREE.` → `ENDINGS AND KEEPINGS, CLOSE TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: The words are sarab kaal and sarab paal. Sarab means all, everything. Kaal you met eleven days ago: time, and death, the thing that ends. Paal is the root of paalna, the Punjabi word for raising a child, feeding, protecting, keeping alive. So Jaap salutes the One as the ending of all things and the keeping of all things. Now put this beside the first word of the glide. On day three hundred thirty-seven, Jaap bowed to akaal, the One without kaal, beyond time and death. Here the same One is called the kaal of everything. Is that a contradiction? Not in the way Sikh scripture reads it. In Sikh teaching, the One isn't subject to time, but every ending in time happens within the One's order. Sikhs call that order hukam. Guru Nanak's Japji says everything is within hukam, and nothing is outside it. Births, deaths, harvests, partings: all inside. The Tenth Guru is willing to call the One by the hard name too. In other parts of his writing he speaks of the One as Kaal and Mahakaal, great Time, the power that brings all things to their close. He doesn't pretend endings aren't real, or that they come from somewhere else. But here Jaap doesn't say sarab kaal alone. It comes with sarab paal. The hand that ends is the same hand that keeps. The leaf falls, and the soil feeds the tree. For Sikhs living through an ending, that pairing can be a quiet comfort: in Jaap, the One who closes doors is also the One who keeps.
screen: `SARAB KAAL: THE ENDING OF ALL.` · `SARAB PAAL: THE KEEPING OF ALL.` · `HUKAM: NOTHING OUTSIDE THE ORDER.` · `THE HAND THAT ENDS ALSO KEEPS.` · then, large: `ENDS AND KEEPS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one ending and one beginning. Think back over this week. Find one thing that ended: a project, a season, a habit, a conversation, maybe a relationship. Hold it gently for a breath. Now find one thing that began, even something small: a new routine, a new person, a plant sprouting. Hold that too. Let them sit side by side, without choosing between them. If you pray, you can place both in the same hand. The bell holds the time.
Ender and sustainer of all. Sarab kaal, sarab paal: the One who brings every ending and keeps every life, in one breath.
screen: `ENDER AND SUSTAINER OF ALL — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: ends and keeps. Today, when something ends, look for what it's quietly feeding. Day three hundred forty-eight.

349.title: House of compassion
349.hook: karunaalay hain: He is the home of compassion (Jaap, harbolmana)
349.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the quick harbolmana lines of Jaap Sahib each morning, and daya, compassion, is taught as one of the core virtues alongside truth, contentment, humility and love.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ender and sustainer of all, sarab kaal, sarab paal, and your line, ends and keeps. Did an ending show you what it was feeding? Today, a new quick meter, and a house. Day three hundred forty-nine.

Some people have one kitchen like this. A grandmother's, an aunt's, a friend's mom's. You could show up unannounced, any hour, after any kind of day, and the kettle went on before you'd finished saying hello. Nobody asked what you'd done wrong. Nobody made you earn the chair. You just came in, and you were cared for, because that's what the house was for. Some people are kind now and then. Some people are a place you can go. Jaap Sahib names the One like that second kind. Today: house of compassion.
screen: `ONE KITCHEN YOU COULD ALWAYS GO TO.` → `THE KETTLE WENT ON BEFORE HELLO.` → `SOME PEOPLE ARE A PLACE.`

segments.voice: Jaap shifts into yet another meter, harbolmana, with tiny, fast lines of just two words each, and the first of them is karunaalay hain. It's two words fused. Karunaa is compassion, the feeling that moves toward someone's suffering. Aalay, from aalaya, is a dwelling, a home. That second word hides in the name of a mountain range: Himalaya is hima, snow, plus aalaya, home. The home of snow. So karunaalay is the home of compassion. You are the house where compassion lives. That's a different picture from compassionate. A compassionate person feels it sometimes, in a good mood, on a good day. A home of compassion is where it lives all the time, whether anyone visits or not. It's the kitchen where the kettle is always ready. Sikhs have a word close to karunaa that they use for a human virtue: daya, kindness, mercy. It's often listed among the virtues a Sikh tries to grow, with truth, contentment, humility and love. And Guru Nanak gives daya a startling job. In Japji, he takes the old myth of a bull holding the earth on its back and says: the bull is dharma, righteousness, and dharma is the child of daya, of compassion. Compassion, in other words, is what holds the world up. So when Jaap calls the One the house of compassion, it's also hinting at what a Sikh home and a Sikh heart might try to be. Not kind sometimes. A place people can come.
screen: `HARBOLMANA: TWO QUICK WORDS A LINE.` · `KARUNAA: COMPASSION. AALAY: HOME.` · `NOT KIND SOMETIMES: A PLACE TO COME.` · `DAYA: THE CHILD WHO HOLDS UP THE WORLD.` · then, large: `HOME OF COMPASSION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be a home of compassion once. Think of someone who might need a place to land right now: a friend going through something, a coworker who's struggling, a relative who's lonely. Picture them walking into a warm kitchen, and picture yourself putting the kettle on. Breathe slowly. Then decide one small way to be that place for them today: a message, a call, a door left open. If you pray, you can say karunaalay hain. The bell holds the time.
Karunaa. Compassion, the feeling that moves toward suffering; and in Jaap, karunaalay, the One as the home where compassion always lives.
Your line: home of compassion. Today, be the kitchen someone can walk into: open your door, your phone, or your attention to one person who needs it. Day three hundred forty-nine.

350.title: Breaker of the cruel
350.hook: khal khanddan hain, mahi manddan hain: He breaks the cruel and adorns the earth (Jaap, harbolmana)
350.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the harbolmana lines, karunaalay hain, khal khanddan hain, mahi manddan hain, briskly each morning in Jaap Sahib, and the saint-soldier ideal joins compassion with standing up to cruelty.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karunaa, and your line, home of compassion. Were you a kitchen someone could walk into? Today, the same quick stanza keeps going, and it gets fierce. Day three hundred fifty, the end of a week.

Anyone who has kept a garden knows the two jobs. One is planting: seeds, bulbs, the hopeful part. The other is pulling. Bindweed wrapping around the beans. A vine strangling the rosebush. Pull them, and the garden breathes again. Skip it, and no amount of planting will save it. A good gardener is gentle and ruthless at the same time, and nobody calls that a contradiction. It's just what loving a garden looks like. Jaap Sahib puts both jobs into a single rhyme. Today: breaker of the cruel.
screen: `A GARDEN HAS TWO JOBS.` → `PLANTING, AND PULLING.` → `GENTLE AND RUTHLESS AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Right after karunaalay, the home of compassion, the harbolmana lines go on: khal khanddan hain, mahi manddan hain. Khal is the cruel one, the wicked, the person who preys on others. Punjabi still uses it for a scoundrel. Khanddan is breaking, shattering. Then mahi is the earth, and manddan is adorning, decorating, making beautiful. The two halves rhyme, khanddan, manddan, and the rhyme is the teaching. Breaking the cruel and adorning the earth aren't two different jobs. They're one job, like pulling the bindweed so the roses can bloom. Notice where this line sits. Directly after compassion. Jaap doesn't separate them. In the Tenth Guru's world, compassion that never stood up to cruelty would be a kitchen with the door open to thieves. The Sikh ideal of the saint-soldier, gentle in the heart and ready in the hands, is in these four tiny lines. And the breaking is never the point on its own. The goal is a more beautiful earth. Cruelty gets broken so that the world can be adorned: fed, sheltered, made fair. And this is where the week ends. Six days ago, Jaap switched into Persian and called the One the lamp of beauty. Then the provider, giver of daily bread. Gobind, generous and infinite. One form, seen in countless ways. The ender and sustainer of all. The house of compassion. And today, the breaker of the cruel, who adorns the earth.
screen: `KHAL KHANDDAN: BREAKING THE CRUEL.` · `MAHI MANDDAN: ADORNING THE EARTH.` · `ONE JOB, LIKE WEEDING A GARDEN.` · `RIGHT AFTER COMPASSION.` · then, large: `BREAK CRUELTY, ADORN EARTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: refuse one small cruelty. Think about the day ahead. Where might a little cruelty show up? A joke at someone's expense in a group chat. Gossip at lunch. A sharp tone with someone who can't answer back. Your own inner voice, being harsh with you. Pick one. Picture it coming, and picture yourself not joining in, or gently changing the subject. Then picture one thing you could make a little more beautiful instead. Breathe. The bell holds the time.
Breaker of the cruel. Khal khanddan, mahi manddan: the One who shatters cruelty and adorns the earth, in a single rhyme.
Your line: break cruelty, adorn earth. Today, refuse one small cruelty, and make one small thing more beautiful. Day three hundred fifty. A week, done.

screen: `DAY 350 COUNTS.` → `A THIRD WEEK OF JAAP.` → `TOMORROW: THE ONE-LETTER METER.`

fork.setup: you're a gardener who loves your roses. bindweed is strangling them. what does loving the garden look like?
options: leave everything alone.
pull the weed so the roses can bloom.
plant more roses and ignore the weed.
fork.reveal: khal khanddan, mahi manddan: breaking what's cruel and adorning the earth are one act of care.

trapdoor: what you thought: breaker of the cruel is a warlike title.
what it means: the One shatters cruelty so the earth can be adorned, and the line sits right after compassion.
what a scholar hears: the harbolmana quatrain pairs karunaalay with ari ghaalay and khal khanddan with mahi manddan, rhyming destruction and adornment.
